name: The Fastest Runners
scope: Land-speed anatomy, animal by animal. Cheetah (Acinonyx jubatus): the flexible spine that folds and unfurls like a spring so all four feet leave the ground twice per stride; semi-retractable claws that grip like running spikes; the enlarged nostrils and heart that let it hit ~100 km/h for only ~20-30 seconds before overheating forces a stop. The pronghorn (Antilocapra americana): not the fastest sprinter but the endurance champion, holding ~55 km/h for miles on oversized lungs and heart — built to outrun an American cheetah that has been extinct for 10,000 years, so it now runs from a ghost. Greyhound double-suspension gallop as the domestic echo. Ostrich as the fastest two-legged runner. Top rung: the cheetah's tail as a rudder that counter-swings to steer high-speed turns.
source: Wilson et al. 2013 Nature (cheetah hunt dynamics); Byers 'Built for Speed' (pronghorn); Britannica; Smithsonian
framing_note: Scene-led: lead with the running body, not 'how fast is a cheetah.' The spring-spine and the pronghorn-outrunning-a-ghost are the memorable handles (VIVID ADAPTATION). Cold speed numbers only when the stem constructs them (the 20-second overheating limit is a real constraint that pays off, not orphan trivia). The extinct-American-cheetah payoff is animal-anchored human/deep-time drama, not filler.

name: Champion Jumpers
scope: The physics of the leap across animals that store and release energy. Froghopper/spittlebug (Philaenus spumarius): the true jump champion by acceleration, catapulting with a latch-and-release mechanism (resilin, a near-perfect rubber protein) at ~400 g. Flea: a similar spring-loaded resilin pad in the leg, leaping ~100+ times its body length. Grasshopper's semi-lunar catapult in the knee. Kangaroo (Macropus): the opposite trick — huge elastic tendons in the legs act as pogo springs so hopping gets MORE efficient at speed, the tail as a fifth 'leg' that pushes off. Bush baby / galago spring-loaded leaps. Top rung: why muscle alone can't do it — a latch/spring beats muscle because muscle contracts too slowly, so tiny animals store energy first and release it in an instant.
source: Burrows (froghopper/planthopper jump mechanics, J. Exp. Biol.); Bennet-Clark (flea resilin); Dawson & Taylor 1973 (kangaroo hopping energetics); Britannica
framing_note: The wonder is the LATCH-AND-SPRING (a catapult, not a muscle) — that is the vivid adaptation the whole ladder deepens. Kangaroo pogo-tendon is the mammal counterpoint. g-forces are numbers only where the stem builds them; the resilin 'rubber protein' is a named concrete handle. Do not anthropomorphize; state the mechanism as physics.

name: Moving Without Legs
scope: The distinct ways a legless body travels. Serpentine (lateral undulation): the S-wave every snake makes, pushing sideways against irregularities in the ground. Sidewinding: the sidewinder rattlesnake (Crotalus cerastes) throwing loops of itself so only two points touch scorching sand, leaving disconnected J-tracks. Rectilinear 'caterpillar' creep: a heavy python moving in a straight line by pulling its belly scales forward in waves — how a big constrictor stalks unseen. Concertina: bunching and extending to climb a smooth tube or branch. Belly scales (scutes) as the grip that makes it all work. Legless lizards vs snakes as a recognition rung (a 'snake' with eyelids and ear holes is a lizard). Top rung: the flying snake, which flattens into a ribbon and undulates through air — undulation escaping the ground entirely.
source: Jayne (snake locomotion, J. Morphology / J. Exp. Biol.); Britannica; National Geographic
framing_note: Each named gait is one wonder per rung — never staple sidewinding onto a rectilinear rung. Sidewinding-on-hot-sand and the straight-line python stalk are the vivid handles. The flying-snake payoff links to the air-movement strand but stays anchored to how the body actually moves. Keep binomials current.

name: Sticking to Walls
scope: Clinging and climbing without glue. Gecko (e.g. Tokay, Gekko gecko): toe pads covered in millions of microscopic hairs (setae), each splitting into hundreds of tips (spatulae), that grip by van der Waals force — the faint attraction between molecules in contact — so a gecko hangs from glass by one toe and peels free instantly by changing the angle. Tree frog toe-discs that grip by wet adhesion (a thin water film and surface tension), a different trick from the dry gecko. Insects (fly, beetle) using tiny adhesive footpads with sticky fluid. Squid/octopus suckers and a limpet's clamp as the suction counterpoint. Top rung: geckos inspired dry adhesive tape and climbing robots — the science that copied the toe.
source: Autumn et al. 2000/2002 Nature (gecko setae, van der Waals); Britannica; Journal of Experimental Biology
framing_note: The wonder: no glue — molecular stickiness (van der Waals) via a forest of split hairs. Contrast dry gecko grip vs wet tree-frog grip vs suction as three CLEAN mechanisms (one per rung). 'Van der Waals force' is the named concept but teach it as 'molecules touching pull faintly,' not as bare jargon (teach-before-test).

name: Flight Evolved Four Separate Times
scope: Powered flight built independently in four lineages, each with a different wing. Insects (first, ~325+ mya): wings that are outgrowths of the body wall, not modified limbs — so an insect keeps all six legs AND flies. Pterosaurs: a wing membrane stretched from the body to an enormously elongated fourth finger (the 'wing finger'). Birds: feathered wings built on the whole forelimb, with hollow bones and a keeled sternum anchoring flight muscles. Bats (the only flying mammals): a skin membrane stretched between hugely elongated finger bones — a webbed hand for a wing. The concept of convergent evolution: four solutions to the same problem of getting airborne, no shared 'flight ancestor.' Recognition rungs sorting a wing to its owner by its skeleton. Top rung: only these four groups ever achieved true powered flight in 350 million years — everyone else only glides.
source: Britannica; AMNH; Cornell Lab of Ornithology; UCMP Berkeley (pterosaur/bat/insect wing anatomy)
framing_note: Convergence is the spine — the SAME need, FOUR different wings, told through the concrete skeleton each time (insect body-wall flaps vs pterosaur wing-finger vs bird feathered arm vs bat webbed hand). 'Four times' is a number only because the stem constructs the roster. Deep-time framing factual, no theology. This is the recognition base for the whole air strand — keep a strong T1/T2 floor.

name: Hovering in Place
scope: The rare animals that hold still in the air. Hummingbird (Trochilidae): a shoulder joint that rotates so the wing generates lift on BOTH the forward and backward stroke, tracing a figure-8, beating ~50 times a second and letting it fly backward — the only bird that can. The huge breast muscles and a heart beating ~1,200/min to power it, plus the extreme fuel cost that forces nightly torpor. Hawkmoths (Sphingidae) and hoverflies converging on the same figure-8 hover to drink nectar mid-air. Dragonflies hovering with four independently controlled wings. Kestrel 'wind-hovering' — the cheat where the bird hangs on a headwind rather than truly beating in still air. Top rung: hovering is the most energy-expensive way to fly, which is why so few animals can afford it.
source: Britannica; Cornell Lab of Ornithology; Journal of Experimental Biology (hummingbird/hawkmoth aerodynamics)
framing_note: The figure-8 backstroke that also makes lift is the vivid adaptation — that is the fact every rung deepens. Backward flight is the memorable payoff. Distinguish TRUE hovering (figure-8) from the kestrel's headwind cheat as separate rungs. Wingbeat/heart numbers appear only where the stem builds the astonishment; the mechanism leads.

name: Gliding, Not Flying
scope: The many animals that fall with style — no powered flight, just a membrane to slow and steer a downward glide. Flying squirrel: a furred skin flap (patagium) between wrist and ankle, steering with its flat tail. Colugo (Cynocephalus): the champion glider, a membrane from neck to fingertips to tail — the most complete gliding mammal, gliding 100+ m between trees. Flying fish (Exocoetidae): wing-like pectoral fins and a tail that beats the water for a running takeoff, gliding above waves to escape predators. 'Flying' snake (Chrysopelea): flattening its ribs into a ribbon and undulating to glide. Draco lizard: gliding on membranes stretched over elongated ribs. Wallace's flying frog with huge webbed feet. Top rung: gliding evolved over and over because it's cheap — a shortcut to flight's escape-and-travel payoff without the enormous cost of powered wings.
source: Britannica; National Geographic; Journal of Experimental Biology (colugo/Draco/Chrysopelea glide)
framing_note: The distinction gliding-is-not-flying is the whole point — each rung is one animal's membrane and how it steers, one wonder each. Colugo-as-champion and the flattened-ribbon snake are the vivid handles. Do not blur gliders into 'fliers'; the recognition contrast with the four true-flight lineages is a deliberate rung. Keep binomials current.

name: Endurance Aloft
scope: Animals that stay airborne almost without landing. Wandering albatross (Diomedea exulans): the ~3.5 m wingspan (largest of any living bird) and dynamic soaring — stealing energy from the wind gradient over waves to travel thousands of km barely flapping; a shoulder lock that holds the wing open with no muscle effort. Arctic tern (Sterna paradisaea): the longest migration of any animal, pole to pole and back (~70,000+ km a year), so it sees more daylight than any creature on Earth. Common swift (Apus apus): can stay aloft for ~10 months without landing — eating, mating, and sleeping on the wing, half its brain at a time. Frigatebird sleeping mid-flight. Bar-tailed godwit's nonstop trans-Pacific flight (~11,000 km, no food, no water, no rest). Top rung: these birds solved the same problem — cover huge distances without the fuel cost of constant flapping — with wind-riding tricks.
source: Britannica; Cornell Lab of Ornithology; Nature/Science (swift 10-month flight, godwit tracking, tern migration)
framing_note: Dynamic soaring (stealing wind energy) and the swift living 10 months airborne are the vivid adaptations — mechanism first, then the payoff distance. The pole-to-pole tern seeing the most daylight of any animal is a constructed-number wonder, not cold trivia. Keep migration facts current (godwit records updated by satellite tracking); flag ongoing tracking research honestly at top tier.

name: The Tuna Body Plan (Thunniform Swimming)
scope: The torpedo shape that fast open-ocean swimmers keep re-inventing. The thunniform body: a stiff streamlined torso, a narrow tail-base, and a crescent (lunate) tail that sweeps side to side like a propeller — almost no wasted wobble. Tuna (Thunnus): retractable fins that fold into grooves, and warm muscles (partial endothermy) that stay hotter than the sea for extra power. Sharks (mako, great white): the same crescent tail and streamlined body — but a shark sweeps its tail side to side while a dolphin sweeps up and down. Dolphins/whales (mammals): the same torpedo shape, up-down tail. Ichthyosaurs (extinct marine reptiles): the same body plan again, ~90 million years earlier — a reptile shaped like a tuna. The concept: four unrelated lineages (fish, mammal, reptile) converged on ONE best shape for cruising fast in open water. Top rung: side-to-side vs up-and-down tail is the give-away that tells you which lineage you're looking at.
source: Britannica; AMNH; UCMP Berkeley (ichthyosaur convergence); Journal of Experimental Biology (thunniform swimming)
framing_note: Convergence is the spine — the SAME torpedo shape in tuna, shark, dolphin, ichthyosaur, each a concrete animal rung. The crescent tail and the side-to-side (fish/shark/reptile) vs up-and-down (mammal) tell is the vivid, memorable handle. The ichthyosaur-shaped-like-a-tuna deep-time payoff is animal-anchored, factual, no theology. Keep tuna endothermy accurate (regional, not full warm-blood).

name: Jet Propulsion
scope: Animals that swim by squirting water. Squid: draws water into the mantle, then fires it through a steerable funnel (siphon) to rocket backward — the fastest jet swimmers in the sea, some launching clear out of the water to 'fly.' Octopus: the same mantle-and-siphon jet used as an escape burst, aiming the funnel to steer. Nautilus: jets while adjusting gas in its chambered shell for buoyancy. Jellyfish: the bell squeezes and relaxes, pushing a ring of water — the most energy-efficient swimming of any animal, coasting between pulses. Scallop: claps its two shells to jet away from a starfish in clumsy hops — a bivalve that swims. Dragonfly nymph jetting water from its rear. Top rung: a jet trades efficiency for a fast escape (squid/octopus burst) OR maximizes efficiency by coasting (jellyfish) — two ways to use the same principle.
source: Britannica; Journal of Experimental Biology (jellyfish/squid propulsion efficiency); National Geographic
framing_note: One squirting animal per rung — never staple the scallop clap onto the squid rung. The siphon-funnel rocket and the shell-clapping swimming scallop are the vivid handles. The efficiency contrast (jellyfish-most-efficient vs squid-fast-burst) is the payoff concept, animal-anchored. 'Flying squid' launching out of water is a real, memorable T3/T4 rung.

name: Staying Up or Sinking
scope: How animals control their depth without swimming constantly. Bony fish: a gas-filled swim bladder inflated and deflated to hang weightless at any depth — the trick that lets a fish hover. Sharks: NO swim bladder, so they'd sink; instead a huge oil-rich liver (squalene) that's lighter than water gives lift, and many must keep swimming or drop. Sperm whale: the giant spermaceti organ in its head — waxy oil that may be warmed/cooled to shift buoyancy for deep dives (a leading, still-debated idea). Cuttlefish: a porous internal 'cuttlebone' with gas-filled chambers, ballast tuned like a submarine. Deep-sea fish with reduced or oil-filled bladders. Krill and larvae using oil droplets for lift. Top rung: gas (swim bladder, cuttlebone) vs oil (shark liver, spermaceti) — two solutions to the sink-or-float problem, and gas fails a fish hauled up fast from the deep.
source: Britannica; AMNH; Journal of Experimental Biology; Marine biology texts (spermaceti buoyancy hypothesis noted as debated)
framing_note: The swim-bladder-hovering fish and the shark's oily liver are the vivid handles; gas-vs-oil is the organizing contrast (one mechanism per rung). Flag the spermaceti buoyancy idea honestly as a leading-but-debated hypothesis (research-in-progress), not settled fact. Numbers only where the stem constructs them. Keep binomials/taxonomy current.

name: Deep-Diving Bodies
scope: How air-breathing animals survive crushing dives. Sperm whale (Physeter macrocephalus): dives ~2,000 m for over an hour hunting giant squid; its ribcage and lungs collapse on the way down (so there's little air to crush or dissolve dangerously), and its muscles are packed with myoglobin — so dark it's nearly black — storing oxygen in the muscle itself. Weddell/elephant seals: heart rate crashes (bradycardia) and blood is shunted to brain and heart while limbs go without, plus a huge blood volume as an oxygen tank. Cuvier's beaked whale: the record diver, ~3,000 m and ~3.7 hours. Avoiding the bends: collapsed lungs stop nitrogen from dissolving into blood under pressure — the trap that kills human divers. Top rung: these divers store oxygen in blood and MUSCLE, not the lungs — the opposite of how a human holds a breath.
source: Britannica; Kooyman & Ponganis (diving physiology); Nature/Science (Cuvier's beaked whale dive records); Smithsonian
framing_note: Collapsing lungs, myoglobin-black muscle, and the dive reflex are the vivid adaptations — each a clean rung, mechanism first. The 'avoiding the bends by NOT holding air' payoff is the counter-intuitive hook, contrasted with human divers (animal-anchored human drama, not filler). Depth/time are constructed numbers that carry the wonder. Keep dive records current; note beaked-whale physiology is still actively researched.

name: Filter Feeding the Ocean
scope: The biggest animals eating some of the smallest, by straining. Baleen whales (blue, humpback, right): no teeth — instead curtains of baleen (keratin, the stuff of fingernails) that sieve krill and small fish from a giant gulp of water; the blue whale, the largest animal that ever lived, lives on tiny krill this way. Humpback bubble-net feeding as the cooperative twist. Whale shark and basking shark: the biggest fish, cruising with mouths open, straining plankton through gill rakers. Flamingo: feeds UPSIDE-DOWN, its bent bill a sieve pumped by the tongue to strain brine shrimp and algae from mud — and those shrimp are what turn it pink. Manta ray and crabeater seal (lobed teeth as a krill sieve) as further rungs. Top rung: the largest bodies on Earth are built by filtering the smallest food — a paradox with the same solution (a built-in sieve) in whales, sharks, and birds.
source: Britannica; AMNH; Smithsonian; Cornell Lab of Ornithology (flamingo feeding)
framing_note: The biggest-eats-smallest paradox is the spine; one filter-feeder per rung. Baleen-is-fingernail-keratin, upside-down flamingo, and the pink-comes-from-shrimp are the vivid, memorable handles (the flamingo color is a coherent single-fact payoff, not stapled trivia). Blue-whale-largest-ever is a constructed superlative, not cold number. Keep the sieve mechanism (baleen vs gill rakers) distinct per lineage.

name: Teeth Built for the Job
scope: How a tooth's shape reveals a diet. Carnivore: bladelike carnassial cheek teeth that shear past each other like scissors to slice meat and crack bone (cat, wolf), plus stabbing canines. Herbivore: broad flat-ridged molars that grind tough plants, and a gap (diastema) where meat-teeth would be (horse, cow, deer). Rodents: chisel incisors that NEVER stop growing, worn sharp by constant gnawing — a beaver or rat must gnaw or its teeth grow into its own skull; the front enamel is iron-hardened orange. Elephant tusks as overgrown incisors, and molars that conveyor-belt: worn ones fall out the front as new ones push in from behind, six sets in a lifetime, then starvation. Shark teeth in endless replacing rows, ~30,000 in a lifetime. Top rung: you can read what an animal eats from a single tooth — slicer, grinder, or ever-growing chisel.
source: Britannica; AMNH; Smithsonian (dental anatomy, elephant molar succession, rodent incisor growth)
framing_note: Read-the-diet-from-the-tooth is the spine; slicer vs grinder vs ever-growing chisel are three clean recognition rungs (strong T1/T2 base). Ever-growing rodent incisors (gnaw or die) and the elephant's six molar sets then starvation are the vivid, single-fact payoffs — each its own rung, not stapled. Iron-orange rodent enamel is a concrete named handle. Keep the carnassial/diastema terms taught-before-tested.

name: Venom for the Hunt
scope: Chemical weapons for killing prey (and defense). Snakes: hollow or grooved fangs injecting venom — vipers with long folding fangs (Gaboon viper's ~5 cm), cobras that can spit venom into eyes; venom types that either destroy tissue (hemotoxic) or shut down nerves (neurotoxic). Cone snail (Conus): a fish-hunting sea snail that harpoons prey with a modified tooth loaded with fast-acting venom — some potent enough to kill a person; a slow reef snail that out-drugs a fish. Box jellyfish (Chironex fleckeri): tentacles studded with stinging cells (nematocysts) that fire like microscopic harpoons — among the most venomous animals alive. Blue-ringed octopus: tiny, carries tetrodotoxin, flashes its rings as a warning. Platypus: a venomous spur on the male's hind leg — a venomous MAMMAL. The distinction venom (injected) vs poison (eaten/touched). Top rung: venom is a way to subdue prey too big or fast to overpower — chemistry replacing muscle.
source: Britannica; AMNH; Australian Museum; toxinology reviews (Conus, Chironex, Ornithorhynchus venom)
framing_note: One venomous hunter per rung; the injected-vs-eaten (venom vs poison) distinction is a deliberate teaching rung. The cone snail harpooning a fish, the nematocyst microscopic harpoon, and the venomous male platypus are the vivid handles. Fang/potency numbers only where the stem builds them. Do not sensationalize danger to humans — frame as the animal's hunting tool. Keep binomials current.

name: Squeezing, Not Biting
scope: How constrictors actually kill — the myth-buster ladder. Boa, python, anaconda: they do NOT crush or suffocate by breaking bones; each time the prey exhales, the coils tighten a notch, and the real, fast killer is stopping blood flow — cutting off circulation to the brain and heart so the animal blacks out in seconds (a modern finding that overturned the old 'suffocation' story). Backward-curved teeth that grip but don't chew — the whole meal goes down head-first, whole. A jaw with a stretchy ligament (not 'unhinging') and skin that spreads to swallow prey wider than the snake's own head. Green anaconda (Eunectes murinus) as the heaviest. Reticulated python as the longest. Top rung: a constrictor eats one big meal and then may not eat again for weeks or months, its gut and heart growing to digest, then shrinking back.
source: Boback et al. 2015 (constriction stops circulation, not breathing); Britannica; National Geographic
framing_note: The circulation-not-suffocation finding is the wonder and the myth-buster — lead with it, cite it as a recent discovery correcting the old story (research honestly flagged). Jaw-ligament (not 'unhinging') corrects a second myth. One fact per rung. The eat-once-then-fast payoff is an animal-anchored physiology rung, not filler. No danger sensationalism.

name: Remarkable Tongues
scope: Tongues rebuilt into tools. Chameleon: a tongue launched over a body-length in a hundredth of a second — a spring-loaded catapult (elastic collagen wound like a rubber band, then released) with a suction-cup, sticky tip that snatches an insect faster than the eye can follow. Woodpecker: a tongue so long it wraps up and over the back of the skull, anchored between the eyes — extra length to spear grubs deep in wood, and the wrapping also helps cushion the brain against hammering. Anteater/pangolin: a ~60 cm sticky tongue flicked in and out ~150 times a minute to lap up ants, with no teeth at all. Nectar bats and hummingbirds with brush/pump tongues. Frog/toad's sticky flip-out tongue. Top rung: a tongue can be a catapult, a harpoon, or a glue-mop — each shaped by exactly what it must catch.
source: Britannica; de Groot & van Leeuwen (chameleon tongue mechanics); Cornell Lab (woodpecker tongue); Smithsonian
framing_note: The chameleon catapult-tongue and the woodpecker tongue wrapping around the skull are the standout vivid handles — one tongue-tool per rung. Catapult / harpoon / glue-mop is the organizing frame (recognition-friendly, good T1/T2 rungs). Speed and length numbers only where the stem constructs the astonishment. State the spring/collagen mechanism as physics, no anthropomorphizing.

name: Beaks for Every Meal
scope: How a bird's bill matches its food. Darwin's finches (Galapagos): closely related species with bills scaled from a heavy nut-cracker to a fine insect-tweezer — the living demonstration that shape follows diet, and that beaks can shift within a few dry years (the Grants' 40-year study). Raptor hook: eagle/hawk bills curved to tear flesh. Crossbill: mandible tips that cross like scissors to pry open pine cones — a bird with a deliberately 'deformed' bill that fits one job perfectly. Hummingbird's needle for deep flowers (the sword-billed hummingbird's bill longer than its own body). Pelican's throat pouch, spoonbill's sieve-sweep, toucan's huge light bill (which doubles as a heat radiator). Woodpecker chisel. Top rung: give the same island a dozen foods and evolution carves a dozen bills — one beak, one meal.
source: Britannica; Cornell Lab of Ornithology; Grant & Grant 'How and Why Species Multiply' (Galapagos finches); Smithsonian
framing_note: Shape-follows-food is the spine; one bill/one meal per rung, recognition-friendly (strong T1/T2 base). The crossed crossbill tips and the sword-billed hummingbird's over-body-length bill are the vivid handles. Darwin's-finches evolution stated as standard biology (the Grants' real-time measurements are the payoff), no theology. Toucan-bill-as-radiator is a clean single-fact rung.

name: Digesting Grass (The Ruminant's Four Stomachs)
scope: How grass-eaters unlock food no animal can digest alone. Ruminants (cow, deer, giraffe, sheep): a four-chambered stomach whose first, huge chamber (the rumen) is a fermentation vat where trillions of microbes break down cellulose — the animal can't digest grass, its microbe partners do. Chewing the cud: swallowed grass is fermented, burped back up, chewed again, and re-swallowed — that's what a resting cow is doing. Grazing-anatomy payoff: the whole reason to eat fast then chew safely later is to graze in the open and retreat before a predator strikes. The gut microbes as the real digesters (and the methane they burp). Hindgut fermenters (horse, rabbit) as the alternative — rabbits re-eating special soft droppings (cecotrophy) to get a second pass. Top rung: no grazing mammal makes its own cellulose-cutting enzyme — every one of them rents gut microbes to do it.
source: Britannica; Van Soest 'Nutritional Ecology of the Ruminant'; Smithsonian
framing_note: The microbes-do-the-digesting partnership is the wonder — the animal can't break down grass, its tenants can. Cud-chewing and the eat-fast/chew-safe grazing payoff are clean single-fact rungs. Rabbit cecotrophy is a memorable contrast rung. Keep the four chambers taught-before-tested; state fermentation as biology (methane included, factual, no climate editorializing).

name: Lures & Ambush
scope: Predators that bring the prey to them. Deep-sea anglerfish (Melanocephalus / Ceratiidae): a fishing-rod spine tipped with a glowing lure (light from bacteria living in the bulb) dangled before a huge mouth in the lightless deep — food is lured into the dark maw. Alligator snapping turtle (Macrochelys temminckii): lies still on the bottom with mouth open, wiggling a pink worm-shaped lump on its tongue; a fish swims in to eat the 'worm' and the jaws snap. Spider-tailed viper (Pseudocerastes urarugensis): a tail tip shaped and moved exactly like a spider to lure insect-eating birds within striking range. Frogfish/stonefish dangling a lure while camouflaged as rock. Bolas spider swinging a scented glue-ball to catch a specific moth. Photuris firefly females flashing the mating code of another species to lure and eat the males. Top rung: an ambush lure is a trap that costs almost no energy — the predator becomes bait.
source: Britannica; AMNH; Journal of Zoology (spider-tailed viper; anglerfish esca); Smithsonian
framing_note: The predator-becomes-bait idea is the spine; one lure per rung — the glowing anglerfish esca, the snapping turtle's worm-tongue, the spider-mimicking viper tail are the vivid handles. The bacterial-light source of the anglerfish lure is a single-fact rung (links the making-light strand but stays anchored here). Femme-fatale firefly is a memorable T4. Keep binomials current; state mimicry as evolved form, not intent.
